q: How does STALK-style surrogate-Hessian parallel line search scale to deep variational circuits with 100s to 1000s of parameters (e.g. deep ADAPT-VQE, hardware-efficient with many layers, chemistry ansatze on H4/cc-pVDZ with 193 params or beyond), and how does the observed 2-4x speedup versus Powell hold up against strong gradient-based baselines (SPSA, Adam with parameter-shift, quantum natural gradient descent) that are actually engineered for noisy quantum gradients rather than the scipy defaults benchmarked in the paper?
basis: Gustafson et al. (2025) headline speedup numbers are demonstrated at up to 193 parameters and on shallow hardware-efficient ansatze; the paper's baselines are scipy Powell/BFGS/COBYLA/CG/SLSQP/ExcitationSolve, not SPSA/Adam-parameter-shift/QNGD. Surrogate Hessian cost scales at least O(p^2) function calls for finite-difference and eigendecomposition is O(p^3); at 500-1000 parameters this may swamp any wins from fewer line-search evaluations. In this replication only Ns=4 (4 params) is tested, so the scaling claim itself is unprobed.
next_steps: Build an MPS(bond-4)-surrogate + exact-statevector-noisy-high-level rig on uicgpu; sweep parameter counts p in {28, 55, 100, 193, 400, 800} for a shared TFIM/UCCSD family; report (a) surrogate Hessian build cost, (b) LS calls to reach fixed epsilon, (c) SPSA/Adam-parameter-shift/QNGD wall-clock baselines with tuned learning rate; produce a p-vs-total-cost plot (calls and wall-clock) showing the crossover point where surrogate LS stops winning.

q: Does the surrogate optimizer's noise-resilience advantage survive under realistic NISQ noise models that include coherent crosstalk, non-Markovian dephasing, gate-dependent errors, and correlated readout noise, or does it only hold under the paper's implicit additive-Gaussian / depolarizing-Pauli noise assumption?
basis: Gustafson et al. model sampling noise as (effectively) additive-Gaussian on the cost, and the QPU section mitigates errors via DD + readout mitigation + ZNE + PEC + Clifford rescaling before comparing to MPS reference. This is much cleaner than raw NISQ noise. The surrogate LS argument depends on the noisy-high-level being an unbiased estimator of the smooth surrogate landscape near the current point; coherent errors and crosstalk introduce systematic bias that breaks that assumption, and this is not stress-tested in the paper. This replication used simple additive Gaussian sigma=5e-4, which is the paper's noise model.
next_steps: Extend qiskit-aer noise model to include: (i) two-qubit ZZ crosstalk on idle qubits during entangling gates, (ii) T2* fluctuation drawn from a 1/f spectrum, (iii) correlated readout error M matrix with off-diagonal weight ~5%, (iv) coherent over-rotation on entangling gates ~1% amplitude; rerun SurrogateLS + Powell + COBYLA + SPSA sweeps at Ns in {4, 8, 12}; report (a) final energy gap, (b) variance across seeds, (c) whether the surrogate Hessian eigenvector directions computed from the smooth surrogate still align with the noisy landscape's actual descent directions (measure cosine similarity between surrogate-eigenvector-guided step and true steepest-descent step).

q: How well does the surrogate optimizer transfer across related problem instances (e.g. molecule series H2->H2O->N2, active-space sweeps, different bond lengths), and can surrogate models or surrogate-Hessian directions be warm-started or amortized across a family of related instances to pay back their construction cost?
basis: In practice VQE workflows scan potential energy surfaces or sweep active spaces; each new geometry currently costs a full optimization. Gustafson et al. focus on optimizer performance at a single geometry; the paper does not address whether the surrogate Hessian at geometry g_i is a useful warm start for geometry g_{i+1}, or whether a single MPS/SWS surrogate trained on one Hamiltonian family generalizes to a related one. If yes, this could turn per-point 2-4x wins into per-scan 10x+ wins. If no, the surrogate cost has to be paid every time.
next_steps: Take a diatomic bond-length scan (e.g. N2/STO-3G at bond lengths 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0 Angstrom), run SurrogateLS at bond length 0.9, then rerun at each subsequent geometry with three initialization protocols: (a) cold start; (b) warm start parameters only; (c) warm start parameters AND reuse previous surrogate Hessian eigenbasis for the first LS iteration. Report calls-to-convergence and quality of the reused eigenbasis (via subspace-angle metric) as a function of geometry displacement. Extend to different active-space sizes at fixed geometry to test transfer across problem sizes.

q: How does STALK-style surrogate optimization integrate with (and compare against) modern hybrid quantum-classical stacks that have appeared since the paper's cutoff -- QSCI (Quantum Selected CI), ADAPT-VQE variants, QITE (Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution), generative-model-assisted circuit design, quantum subspace diagonalization (QSD) -- and how does it compare to Bayesian-optimization and reinforcement-learning-based optimizer baselines that also target the noisy-black-box regime?
basis: Gustafson et al. benchmark STALK against classical scipy optimizers on a fixed ansatz. They do not compare against GP-BO / Bayesian optimization for VQE (Iannelli & Jansen; Nakaji et al.) or against RL-based VQE optimizers, both of which are the closest cousins to a surrogate-based approach. They also do not address how surrogate LS composes with ADAPT-VQE (where the ansatz is grown adaptively -- Hessian eigenbasis becomes invalid after each grow step) or QSCI (which sidesteps parameterized optimization entirely by sampling and classical diagonalization). Understanding where surrogate LS sits in this taxonomy determines whether it's a niche technique or a broadly useful primitive.
next_steps: Design a common benchmark suite (H2O/STO-3G at 3 geometries) run with (a) STALK-style SurrogateLS, (b) GP-BO with Matern-5/2 kernel and expected-improvement acquisition, (c) an RL-based optimizer (e.g. PPO learning to propose parameter updates from noisy energy history), (d) ADAPT-VQE with surrogate LS invoked after each grow step, (e) QSCI baseline; report calls-to-convergence, final energy gap, and total wall-clock. Publish the harness so the comparison can be extended by others.

q: In the fault-tolerant / logical-qubit era, where circuits are deeper and noise-mitigated to near-exact levels and analytic gradients (parameter-shift, quantum natural gradient) become tractable at reasonable cost, where does surrogate-based optimization remain competitive against pure gradient-based fault-tolerant optimizers, and is STALK a NISQ-era artifact or a durable primitive?
basis: The paper's motivation is that sampling noise kills gradient methods on NISQ devices. In the FT era, sampling noise per Hamiltonian term can be pushed arbitrarily low (at higher shot cost), coherent errors are logically corrected, and parameter-shift gradients become well-defined and accurate. If the surrogate itself remains cheaper than obtaining a high-precision gradient sample, surrogate LS still wins on cost per iteration; if not, it becomes redundant. Neither Gustafson et al. nor this replication addresses this crossover.
next_steps: Build a cost model parameterized by (i) target energy precision epsilon, (ii) number of parameters p, (iii) shots-per-expectation-value N_shots(epsilon), (iv) surrogate cost C_surr(p), (v) parameter-shift gradient cost 2p * N_shots(epsilon); solve for the epsilon threshold below which parameter-shift + Adam or QNGD beats SurrogateLS. Sanity-check the model against small numerical experiments using exact simulation with controlled shot noise sigma sweeping over [1e-2, 1e-6]. Publish a phase diagram of 'SurrogateLS wins' vs 'gradient wins' in the (epsilon, p) plane.
